transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Sam, my friends keep saying they'll start investing once they earn more.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Here's why waiting is expensive. Take two people who each put away 300 dollars a month.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Ana starts at 25. Ben starts at 35. Both stop at 65, and both earn an average of 7 percent a year.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: So Ana just has ten more years of saving.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Ten more years, and only 36,000 dollars more out of her pocket: 144,000 in total against Ben's 108,000.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: But at 65, Ana has about 787,000 dollars. Ben has about 366,000.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: She ends up with more than double, from a quarter more money?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: That's compounding. The returns start earning returns, and the early years have the longest to grow.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: So the cheapest thing you can buy is time. Start small, start now, and raise it when you earn more.

segments.title: Why Waiting to Invest Is Expensive

widgets.context: Sources show the S&P 500 averaged about 10% a year nominal since the 1920s, or roughly 6.6–7% after inflation. So 7% matches the inflation-adjusted stock return, not "investments" in general.

answers.question: Could Ben catch up by saving more each month?
answers.text: Yes, but Ben would need to save much more than double. Using the episode's setup (7% a year, compounded monthly, ending at 65), Ana's $300 a month from 25 grows to about $788,000. Ben would need about $646 a month from 35 to reach the same balance, roughly $346 more than his current $300. This is my own estimate, not a figure from the episode, and it ignores fees, taxes, and inflation.

answers.question: Why does a quarter more money give more than double?
answers.text: Priya's "quarter" is a bit off: Ana contributes 144,000 against Ben's 108,000, roughly a third more. The end balance more than doubles because of compounding. Ana's extra ten years let her early deposits grow at 7% for longer, so she ends with about 787,000 versus Ben's 366,000. The transcript gives these numbers but doesn't walk through the mechanism in detail.

answers.question: How much should I raise my monthly amount when I earn more?
answers.text: Sam doesn't give a specific amount. He only says to start small, start now, and raise it when you earn more. The examples so far use a fixed 300 dollars a month, so no raise rule has been covered yet. If he gives one later in the episode, I'll be able to point to it then.

answers.question: Is a 7 percent average yearly return a realistic assumption?
answers.text: Sam's 7% is an assumption he states as a flat average (11.5 s). Search snippets describe the commonly cited long-run stock return as an inflation-adjusted figure from decades of historical data, and they stress that individual years can swing well above or below it, so no single year is guaranteed. I only saw snippets, not full sources, and the episode hasn't said whether its 7% is real or nominal, so I can't confirm it fits every situation.

answers.question: How do the $300 a month turn into $787,000 for Ana?
answers.text: Ana contributes $300 a month from age 25 to 65 (40 years), about $144,000 in total, and her money earns an average 7% a year. Compounding means each deposit earns returns and those returns earn returns too, so the growth adds up to roughly $787,000. My check assumes monthly deposits compounding at 7%/12 each month; the episode hasn't shown this math yet, and 7% is an average assumption, not a guarantee.

answers.question: What if I can only start with a small amount now?
answers.text: The episode hasn't addressed smaller amounts directly yet. So far, Sam's example shows that starting earlier mattered more than contributing more: Ana put in only $36,000 more than Ben and ended with about $787,000 versus his $366,000. Sam credits compounding, where returns earn returns and early years have the most time to grow. How a smaller monthly amount would play out is not covered up to this point.
